analysis.one_liner: Slashes methane leaks and flaring from oil and gas drilling through strict federal limits.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared a House committee on a narrow 23–20 vote in its final week but never reached the House floor, and the Congress ended with it unpassed.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required oil and gas companies to find and fix methane leaks, capture nearly all the gas they produce on federal land instead of burning or venting it, and pay steep penalties — up to 15 times the market value of gas they vent — for waste. It would also have forced public, online reporting of how much gas each operator loses. The House Natural Resources Committee approved it on a narrow 23–20 vote, but it was reported out at the very end of 2022, placed on the House calendar, and the Congress ended before the full House ever voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: People living near oil and gas operations, who breathe less smog-forming and toxic pollution; communities on the front lines of climate change, since methane is a powerful greenhouse gas; and taxpayers, because gas wasted through venting and flaring on federal land is a public resource that belongs to everyone and the bill would have required operators to capture it and meter it publicly.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities near drilling and the climate

how_it_helps.text: Required EPA regulations cutting oil and gas sector methane emissions at least 65% below 2012 levels by 2025 and 90% below by 2030, covering every segment of the system from production to distribution.

Required operators on federal and Indian lands to capture 85% of produced gas within a year and 99% within five years, banned routine venting and flaring of new wells, and mandated monthly leak inspections with prompt repairs.
Imposed heavy penalties on waste — 15 times market value for vented gas and 3 times for flared gas — plus production restrictions, so wasting a public resource becomes expensive.

Required operators to meter and publicly report all vented, flared, and leaked gas, with the data posted online free of charge in a searchable format, so the public can see who is wasting and polluting.
Reinstated the 2016 Waste Prevention rule, restoring waste-prevention standards that had been rolled back until new rules took effect.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies operating on federal and Indian lands, which would bear the cost of leak-detection programs, capture equipment, metering, and penalties for vented and flared gas; some of those costs could be passed to consumers through energy prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies on federal land

drawbacks.text: The bill set aggressive, quick deadlines: operators would have had to capture 85% of gas within a year of enactment and 99% within five years, replace gas-actuated pneumatic equipment within 180 days of rules, and fix leaks within four weeks. Compliance costs for small and mid-size operators could be substantial and could be passed on in energy prices.

The penalties are steep by design — civil penalties of 15 times the market value of vented gas and 3 times the value of flared gas, plus production restrictions — which critics could argue goes beyond what is needed to deter waste and raises the risk of costly disputes over measurements.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits — large cuts in a potent greenhouse gas, royalties recovered from gas now wasted on public land, and public disclosure of who is leaking what — are substantial and fall on the public side. The costs fall on oil and gas companies, which would face equipment upgrades, capture mandates up to 99%, and steep penalties; some of those costs would be passed to consumers through energy prices, though capturing gas that is currently burned or vented also recovers product the companies can sell. The bill's short timeline (final EPA rules within roughly two years) was ambitious and could have imposed compliance strain, but the design tracked requirements the industry already applies in leading states.

outcome.mechanism: The House Natural Resources Committee approved the bill on a 23–20 vote, but it was reported at the very end of 2022, placed on the calendar, and the two-year Congress ended before the full House could vote on it.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in March 2021 and referred to two House committees; a subcommittee held a hearing the same week.
In April 2021, the Natural Resources Committee ordered the bill reported on a narrow 23–20 vote, but it was not formally reported until December 30, 2022 — the last days of the Congress.
The Energy and Commerce Committee was discharged and the bill was placed on the Union Calendar on December 30, 2022, leaving no time for a floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
The bill never gained a single Republican cosponsor; all 21 cosponsors were Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas operators, which avoid capture mandates, leak inspections, and penalties for venting and flaring, and continue wasting gas on public land without those costs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas operators who waste gas

for.name: House Natural Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Held a markup and ordered the bill reported on a 23–20 vote in April 2021, then formally reported it on December 30, 2022.

for.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Was discharged from the bill on December 30, 2022, clearing it for possible House floor action.

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a Democrat, and the committee vote was 23–20 along the partisan lines of the committee; no Republican supported the bill at any stage.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers, especially those on federal and Indian lands
industries.note: Producers would have faced mandatory gas capture (85% rising to 99%), an end to routine venting and flaring, monthly leak inspections, equipment replacement, and penalties of 15 times the market value of vented gas. Their interest in stopping the bill ran directly against the public's interest in cleaner air and recovered royalties.
The bill's mandates for infrared-camera inspections, metering devices, and upgraded equipment would have created demand for monitoring and capture technology.

industries.industry: Coal, oil, and natural gas transport
industries.note: Methane rules would cover transmission, distribution, and storage, including LNG-handling equipment, adding compliance costs for pipeline and storage operators.
